items.item: Lambda's own mechanics: batch and realtime layers run in parallel, merged at query time

at.step: Reveal: Lambda itself, quoted directly

items.item: The realtime layer's own stack: read/write databases, incremental algorithms, a different reasoning model than the batch layer's pure functions

at.step: Reveal: the realtime layer's own stack, quoted directly

items.item: The batch layer always eventually overrides the realtime layer's results, making the realtime layer's own complexity transient

at.step: Reveal: the batch layer always wins, quoted directly

items.item: Kreps's own restatement of Lambda, attributing it to Marz

at.step: Reveal: Lambda itself, quoted directly

items.item: Lambda's real named cost: maintaining the same transformation logic correctly in two complex distributed systems, called not fixable

at.step: Reveal: Lambda's own restatement and its real cost, quoted directly

items.item: Reprocessing (re-deriving output when code changes) is the real shared challenge both architectures answer

at.step: Reveal: reprocessing as the shared problem, quoted directly

items.item: Kappa's mechanism: retain the full log, start a second instance of the same job from the earliest offset, switch over once caught up

items.item: Kreps himself named this architecture "the Kappa Architecture"

items.item: The first predict (step 3) is red-teamed against the plausible wrong answer that a merge of two independently-computed layers is pure arithmetic and so can't disagree; the reveal at step 5 corrects this by quoting the batch layer's permanent authority over the realtime layer, which is exactly what keeps any disagreement temporary rather than absent

at.step: Predict: does merging two independently-computed layers risk them disagreeing?

items.item: The second predict (step 6) is red-teamed against the plausible wrong answer that the query-time merge step is the expensive part of Lambda; the reveal at step 7 quotes Kreps's own naming of the real cost (maintaining duplicate logic across two systems), which he calls not fixable, directly contradicting the merge-step guess

at.step: Predict: is running the same logic twice the expensive part of Lambda, or is it the merge step?

items.item: The third predict (step 9) is red-teamed against the plausible wrong answer that stream processing can only see new data and therefore can never reprocess history on its own; the reveal at step 10 quotes Kreps's own mechanism (an offset that can be reset to the earliest retained record) directly refuting that assumption

at.step: Predict: could one stream-only pipeline reprocess history without a separate batch system?

items.item: Step 8's reprocessing reveal is kept as its own step, separate from both the dual-logic-cost reveal (step 7) and the Kappa reveal (step 10), because Kreps's own source treats it as the shared problem both architectures answer differently — the bridge between Lambda's cost and Kappa's proposed fix, not a restatement of either

at.step: Reveal: reprocessing as the shared problem, quoted directly

items.item: Step 11's honest-trade reveal deliberately keeps Kreps's efficiency comparison (roughly even) and his actual stated preference (operational simplicity) as two separate claims, since CHAPTER.md's own "why the industry drifted to unified engines" clause is about the second claim, not the first, and collapsing them would misattribute the drift to a performance win Kreps himself does not claim

at.step: Reveal: the honest trade, quoted directly
